858ad645a0.q: What innovative produce and snacking products were showcased at the New England Produce Council show in 2026?

858ad645a0.e: Inside the New England Produce Show 2026: Trends, Innovation, and Industry Insights
f: The New England Produce Council show in August 2026 showcased a diverse lineup of convenience-focused innovations across snacking and ready-to-drink categories. Featured products included Harvest Snaps crispy apple and banana chips, Nature Ripe protein bars, Koya plant-based RTD beverages with 32 grams of protein and creatine, Dole Chop Kits in barbecue ranch flavor, Little Blue Farms salad options, and FNS guacamole and taco kits—all designed to meet the growing demand for grab-and-go, nutrient-dense produce solutions.

Patrick Kelly, who attended the event in Everett, Massachusetts, reported on the breadth of product innovation across multiple categories. The show's exhibitors, as detailed in the episode , demonstrated a clear shift toward convenience-driven formats that align with modern consumer purchasing patterns.

The snacking segment emerged as a major focus area , with brands like Harvest Snaps introducing freeze-dried fruit formats in chip form—crispy textures that appeal to consumers seeking healthier alternatives to traditional packaged snacks. These formats extend shelf life while maintaining nutritional integrity.

In the protein and beverage space, plant-based RTD beverages represented a significant category advancement . Koya's offering specifically combined convenience with functional nutrition by delivering 32 grams of protein per serving alongside creatine supplementation, targeting fitness-conscious and on-the-go consumers alike.

The convenience kit category also gained momentum at the show. Dole Chop Kits and FNS guacamole and taco kits positioned complete meal solutions as ready-to-consume options that reduce preparation time while maintaining fresh produce integrity. Little Blue Farms contributed salad options within the same convenience-forward framework.

These product launches underscore a broader industry theme: the conversation at the New England Produce Council show reflected how producers are investing in generational consumer habits. The emphasis on protein fortification, plant-based formats, and minimal-prep packaging suggests the industry is directly responding to lifestyle shifts toward functional nutrition and convenience.

caa20eda4b.q: How do regional produce trade shows like NEPC benefit suppliers and their client relationships?
caa20eda4b.a: Regional shows enable one-on-one time between vendors, retailers, and wholesalers that larger shows cannot provide. As noted, these regional shows allow you…
caa20eda4b.e: Inside the New England Produce Show 2026: Trends, Innovation, and Industry Insights
f: Regional produce shows like the New England Produce Council (NEPC) provide one-on-one time between vendors, retailers, and wholesalers that larger trade expos simply cannot replicate. These intimate settings enable suppliers to step out of the noise, engage directly with clients, and work together on specific solutions—like custom tray sizes or product configurations—that mass-market platforms make difficult to negotiate and impossible to prioritize.
The intimacy advantage over megashows

Large national expos bring scale, but they dilute focus. At a regional show, you're working in a concentrated mix of actual buyers and suppliers who represent your core market. Patrick Kelly, who has attended NEPC for five years, emphasized that these events allow exhibitors and retailers to get into operational details that require face-to-face attention and trust.

Smaller regional platforms also reduce the logistical burden—travel is shorter, booth costs are lower, and the attendee list is curated around the region's real business needs, as discussed in the episode . This efficiency translates to more meaningful conversations per hour than a vendor would have at Fruit Attraction or a coast-to-coast national show.
Custom solutions and relationship depth

One concrete advantage is the ability to negotiate custom product configurations that mass retailers and wholesalers would never address on a crowded expo floor. A supplier can discuss tray sizes, packaging formats, or seasonal product mixes in real time, with the decision-maker present and available—something nearly impossible at megashows where logistics dominate the agenda.

af190f5230.q: How are kit-based produce products addressing consumer demand for convenience while maintaining cooking involvement?
af190f5230.a: FNS focuses on innovative kit products like guacamole and taco kits that help people save time on prep work like cutting tomatoes and onions into chunks.…
af190f5230.e: Inside the New England Produce Show 2026: Trends, Innovation, and Industry Insights
f: Kit products eliminate the most tedious prep steps—chopping tomatoes, dicing onions—while leaving the actual cooking in the hands of the consumer. By handling ingredient prep upfront, kits let time-strapped home cooks engage in the cooking experience they love without spending hours on preparation.
Meeting the cooking enthusiast with limited time

The core insight behind kit-based produce is straightforward: not everyone wants a fully prepared meal, but almost everyone wishes prep work took less time. As discussed in the episode , FNS and similar innovators recognized that a significant gap exists between those who enjoy cooking and those who have the time to do it.

Guacamole kits and taco kits exemplify this approach. Instead of a consumer buying raw avocados, limes, cilantro, and onions separately and spending time cutting everything down to usable pieces, a kit arrives with components already prepped. The consumer opens the package, adds personal touches (their own spices, a preferred protein, extra fresh herbs if desired), and cooks or assembles their dish.

This model preserves the emotional and tactile satisfaction of cooking while compressing the timeline dramatically. Detailed in this podcast , the strategy assumes that consumers value the cooking act itself—the sizzle of ingredients hitting a pan, the control over seasoning, the confidence of assembly—not necessarily the repetitive, knife-work aspects that slow them down.
Minimal effort, maximum involvement

090f1920b4.q: How are freeze-dried fruit brands positioning themselves in the North American produce market?

f: Crispy Fruit, the number one freeze-dried fruit brand in America , builds market position through single-ingredient products combined with strategic trial pack bundles. They launch multi-fruit trial packs featuring strawberry, pineapple, mango, and apple to acquire new customers, then convert them to full-size, regular-priced repeat purchases.

The freeze-dried produce category sits at the intersection of convenience and health-conscious snacking, a positioning detailed in the episode coverage from the New England Produce Show 2026 . By maintaining product simplicity—each SKU contains nothing but the fruit itself—Crispy Fruit eliminates ingredient clutter and builds trust with consumers increasingly scrutinizing labels.

The trial-and-convert model reflects a clear understanding of consumer behavior in premium snacking. Trial packs bundle four distinct flavors to expose new customers to variety without the financial commitment of buying multiple full-size containers. Once trial customers experience the product and confirm quality, converting them to repeat purchase at standard retail pricing maximizes lifetime value while controlling acquisition costs.

This approach addresses a core challenge in premium frozen and freeze-dried categories: penetration into new retail channels and household baskets. Rather than compete on price or forced promotions, Crispy Fruit leads with product purity and strategic sampling, letting the product itself justify the premium positioning in a competitive North American produce market.
Trial packs drive sampling and retail velocity

The bundle strategy serves dual operational purposes. Trial packs reduce the friction of first purchase for consumers unfamiliar with the brand or category, lowering perceived risk. At the retail level, they drive inventory turnover and shelf visibility faster than single-SKU offerings, which benefits both distributor relationships and retailer margins.

a4cd4e8de2.q: How does wheat straw shortage impact mushroom production costs and availability?
a4cd4e8de2.a: Wheat straw is the primary input for mushroom compost substrate. The United States experienced the worst wheat crop since 1961, which has significantly…
a4cd4e8de2.e: Mushrooms in Focus: Industry Insights with Tony Stackhurski
f: Wheat straw is the essential foundation of mushroom compost substrate, and the United States experienced its worst wheat crop since 1961 . This supply collapse has forced mushroom farms to purchase straw at dramatically elevated prices that bear no relationship to quality, creating an unsustainable cost structure for growers trying to maintain margins.
The substrate dependency no one can escape

Mushroom production operates on a fundamentally different model than most crops. Unlike leafy greens or field vegetables, commercial agaricus mushroom farms depend entirely on controlled indoor environments and specially formulated growing substrates . Wheat straw is not a supplemental input—it is the primary structural material in the compost mix that mushroom mycelium colonizes to produce fruit bodies.

When wheat supply tightens, mushroom growers have no workaround. They cannot substitute materials without compromising yield quality or risking crop failure. This direct dependency on a single commodity puts the entire mushroom economics at the mercy of grain market volatility.
2026 wheat crisis: the worst in 65 years

The 2025 U.S. wheat harvest was the poorest in nearly seven decades , creating an immediate supply shortage that rippled through all downstream industries relying on straw. Mushroom farms competing for available inventory face bidding wars with livestock bedding operations, paper manufacturers, and other industrial users.

9f9ca1f958.q: How does sourcing strategy change when fresh market prices for citrus commodities spike dramatically?
9f9ca1f958.a: When fresh market prices for limes go crazy—such as hitting $80 a box—procurement teams get nervous because growers redirect eliminations to the fresh market instead of juice. This forces buyers to think about counter-seasonal production strategies, such as sourcing from Brazil for lime juice when California supply tightens, and considering suppliers from Spain, Egypt, Turkey, and Argentina to diversify supply and manage commodity price volatility.
9f9ca1f958.e: Lessons from 40 year Veteran Dino Cardelli
f: When fresh market prices for limes spike to $80 a box , growers shift their supply away from juice processors and toward fresh market sales, forcing procurement teams to rethink their entire sourcing playbook. The solution is counter-seasonal diversification: sourcing lime juice from Brazil when California tightens, and building redundancy across Spain, Egypt, Turkey, and Argentina to absorb commodity price shocks.
The Fresh Market Premium Triggers a Supply Redirect

When citrus prices on the fresh market climb dramatically, the economics flip for growers. High fresh-market premiums make it far more profitable to sell citrus as whole fruit than to convert it into juice, a lower-margin product. As a result, growers stop selling to juice processors and redirect their elimination fruit—what would normally go to concentrate facilities—straight to fresh market channels.

This creates an immediate pinch for procurement teams managing juice ingredient sourcing. The supply line they counted on evaporates overnight, and they're suddenly competing with fresh-market buyers for diminishing volumes, driving prices even higher up the chain.
Counter-Seasonal Sourcing and Geographic Arbitrage

As Dino Cardelli explains in the episode , the tactical response is to anchor sourcing in counter-seasonal regions . When California's Central Valley supply tightens due to weather or market shifts, procurement teams turn to Brazil, which has an inverted growing season. This creates a natural hedge: as one region peaks, another is ramping down and can absorb overflow demand.

ed4ad19f51.q: What is the difference between a mentality required for fresh produce procurement versus juice procurement?
ed4ad19f51.a: A juice procurement professional must monitor geopolitical events and global weather patterns differently than fresh buyers. When tropical storms form in the Gulf, juice procurement teams think about where the storm will track and whether it will hit the citrus belt. An earthquake in the Kalima area triggers immediate supplier outreach to assess impact. This global, proactive risk-management mindset differs fundamentally from fresh market thinking.
ed4ad19f51.e: Lessons from 40 year Veteran Dino Cardelli
f: Juice procurement professionals operate under a fundamentally different risk-management paradigm than fresh buyers. They must continuously monitor geopolitical events and global weather patterns —tracking tropical storms in the Gulf to predict citrus belt impact, or assessing earthquakes in the Colima area for immediate supplier disruption—rather than reacting to daily market shifts like fresh market operators do.

This proactive, globally-oriented mentality stems from the nature of juice fruit procurement itself. As a juice procurement professional explained in the episode , when a tropical storm forms in the Gulf, juice teams immediately begin scenario-planning: Where will it track? Will it hit the citrus belt? Which suppliers might be affected? This is not speculation—it's a structured intelligence gathering process that determines procurement decisions weeks or months in advance.

Fresh market procurement, by contrast, reacts to price signals and immediate supply availability. A spike in lime prices or a sudden availability shift reshapes buying patterns within days. But juice procurement cannot operate on that timeline. A juice procurement strategy must account for multi-month supply contracts, ingredient consistency requirements, and the reality that a weather event thousands of miles away can trigger cascading supplier impacts across multiple regions.
Geopolitical risk as a procurement lens

An earthquake in Mexico's Colima area isn't just a regional incident for a juice procurement team—it's an immediate trigger for outreach to every affected supplier, assessing damage, alternate sourcing, and timeline implications. This global, forward-looking risk management mindset differs fundamentally from fresh market thinking, where regional disruptions are absorbed and repriced in real time.

Dino Cardelli, who has spent over 35 years managing procurement across grower, processor, and executive roles for companies including Sun Orchard Juicery, PepsiCo, Tropicana, and Dole, draws this distinction clearly. He has worked and managed projects in over 50 countries, giving him direct exposure to how both market segments operate. The difference isn't in the commodities themselves—it's in the decision-making cadence and the breadth of variables considered at once.

e4fc55d62b.q: How has consolidation in citrus growing and juice processing regions reshaped supply chain complexity?
e4fc55d62b.a: Over the past 15-20 years, the industry has consolidated dramatically. Where there used to be eight to ten different growers in a region, now there are two or three. Similarly, the Mexican juice processing industry went from many small processors to three or four major ones. In the Colima area and along the coast, three or four large consolidated players now dominate, which changes how procurement teams must negotiate and plan supply.
e4fc55d62b.e: Lessons from 40 year Veteran Dino Cardelli
f: Over the past 15–20 years, regional citrus growers have consolidated from eight to ten players down to just two or three , and the Mexican juice processing industry followed the same pattern, fundamentally altering how procurement teams negotiate and plan supply. Large consolidated players now dominate key growing and processing regions, eliminating the flexibility that existed when many smaller operators competed side by side.
From Fragmented Markets to Consolidated Giants

The structural shift in the citrus and juice industry has been dramatic. What once was a landscape of diverse, independent growers and processors—offering procurement teams multiple sourcing options—has narrowed significantly. In regions like Colima and along the Mexican coast, three or four large consolidated players now control the market , compared to the scattered ecosystem that existed two decades ago.

This consolidation extends beyond growers to the juice processing side. The Mexican juice processing sector, historically fragmented across many small operators, has collapsed into just three or four major processors . When processing capacity is concentrated in so few hands, procurement teams lose negotiating leverage and flexibility in supplier selection.
As Dino Cardelli explains in this episode , the market dynamics have shifted from "many choices, many partners" to "take it or leave it with a handful of major suppliers."
Supply Chain Ripple Effects

6aa0b145e8.q: What role did triwall bins play in improving juice fruit quality and storage efficiency in procurement?
6aa0b145e8.a: Dino and Patrick were among the first to introduce triwall bins for juice fruit instead of traditional gondolas. Triwalls could be stored in cold rooms, which meant that when trailers or gondolas were unavailable, teams could retrieve triwalls from the warehouse and dump the fruit. This approach maintained consistent fruit quality and gave procurement teams flexibility in managing logistics—plus they achieved rejection rates of less than 1% because they were able to control conditions and inspect loads in person.
6aa0b145e8.e: Lessons from 40 year Veteran Dino Cardelli

453b7604da.q: How did yield-based pricing models align supplier incentives with juice quality specifications?
453b7604da.a: Dino created spreadsheets that tied price to yield: if a supplier could guarantee higher gallons-per-ton output, they could earn a premium price. This incentivized growers to send the best quality fruit, because better fruit meant higher juice yields and higher revenue for both parties. The model worked so well with triwalls because both parties could control and measure the actual yield outcomes.

9ab9293253.q: What does modern citrus procurement knowledge require that technology and spreadsheets alone cannot provide?

13ffe09eb2.q: What is El Niño according to scientific definition and how does it form in the Pacific Ocean?
13ffe09eb2.a: El Niño is a climate pattern that forms when equatorial Pacific Ocean temperatures rise at least 0.5 degrees Celsius above average for several consecutive months. When the Walker Circulation breaks down and warm water shifts east towards South America, El Niño is officially declared.
13ffe09eb2.e: Super El Niño Is Here: Weather, Crops & Global Food Risks
f: El Niño is a climate pattern officially declared when equatorial Pacific Ocean temperatures rise at least 0.5 degrees Celsius above average for several consecutive months . The pattern forms when the Walker Circulation—the normal atmospheric circulation pattern over the Pacific—breaks down, allowing warm water to shift eastward toward South America instead of staying in the western Pacific.
How the Pacific's Circulation System Breaks Down

The Walker Circulation is normally a consistent atmospheric feature that drives trade winds westward and maintains cold water near South America. When this circulation weakens or reverses, warm water pools that usually sit near Indonesia and the western Pacific begin moving across the ocean toward the east coast . This eastward migration is the hallmark of El Niño formation.

The scientific definition relies on precise measurement. As Patrick Kelly explains in the episode , meteorologists track sea surface temperature anomalies in specific Pacific regions using data from organizations like NOAA and the World Meteorological Organization. When those anomalies cross the 0.5-degree threshold and persist across multiple months, the pattern transitions from a forecast concern to an officially declared El Niño event.

Walker Circulation: The normal atmospheric circulation pattern over the Pacific Ocean that typically drives trade winds westward and maintains a temperature gradient, with cooler water in the eastern Pacific and warmer water in the western Pacific. When this circulation breaks down or reverses, warm water migrates east and El Niño conditions develop. This classification system matters because it triggers monitoring and forecasting by major meteorological institutions worldwide. The World Food Program, the Conference Board, and agricultural organizations use El Niño declarations to assess global risks—particularly for food security in vulnerable regions. The podcast covers how current El Niño conditions are already reshaping agricultural forecasts and supply chain planning for 2027.
The Current Super El Niño Event

f00bc2d55c.q: Why is the 2026-2027 El Niño event considered historically significant compared to previous events?

f00bc2d55c.e: Super El Niño Is Here: Weather, Crops & Global Food Risks
f: Forecasts are predicting that this year's El Niño will be the strongest in record history . The World Meteorological Organization has confirmed that El Niño is firmly established and expected to strengthen further, with nearly 100 percent likelihood that it will persist through February 2027—marking the first time the WMO has issued such an unequivocal update.

The 2026–2027 event stands apart from previous El Niño cycles because of the unprecedented certainty and strength that scientific bodies like the World Meteorological Organization have attributed to it. In the past, forecasts carried more hedging language and lower confidence levels. This time, the WMO's near-total confidence in both the establishment and persistence of El Niño through early 2027 signals a rare alignment of atmospheric and oceanic conditions that leave little room for doubt.

What makes this particular cycle historically significant is not just its predicted intensity, but its cascading impact across global food systems . El Niño is expected to peak between September and December 2026, with effects continuing well into 2027. As detailed in this episode of The Produce Industry Podcast , the World Food Program projects that 49 million additional people could face acute food insecurity by the end of 2027.

The agricultural fallout is already being modeled. Central America is facing an 83 percent increase in food insecurity , while East and South Africa expect 18 million people to be affected. Global rice prices are projected to rise between 10 and 20 percent due to yield losses tied to this event. These figures underscore why the produce industry is tracking this cycle so closely.

Patrick Kelly explores the deeper mechanics and regional vulnerabilities of this Super El Niño cycle in the full episode , including how supply chain disruptions may unfold through the end of the decade.
Why the WMO's language matters

89b6bde9ab.q: What weather pattern impacts does El Niño typically produce across the United States?
89b6bde9ab.a: El Niño brings warmer winters in the northern U.S., wetter and cooler winters in the southern U.S., increased likelihood of rain, snow, and tornadoes in wetter regions, stormier weather across the southern U.S., high tide flooding risk on the west coast, changes in fish migration impacting marine ecosystems, and increased formation of harmful algal blooms along the West Coast.
89b6bde9ab.e: Super El Niño Is Here: Weather, Crops & Global Food Risks
f: El Niño creates starkly divided weather impacts across the United States: the northern U.S. experiences warmer, drier winters while the southern regions face wetter, cooler conditions with elevated tornado and severe storm risk. Coastal areas, particularly the West Coast, face increased high tide flooding, and marine ecosystems respond with shifts in fish migration and harmful algal bloom formation.
Regional weather shifts reshape the American landscape

The geographic split is the most striking feature of El Niño's influence. Northern states benefit from warmer winters , reducing heating demand and creating milder conditions, while southern states face the opposite pattern—cooler, wetter winters that drive precipitation spikes and storm activity. This counterintuitive contrast reflects El Niño's disruption of the Walker Circulation, the major atmospheric circulation pattern that normally steers weather systems across the Pacific and into North America.

As detailed in this episode of The Produce Industry Podcast , the southern United States enters a heightened alert state for severe weather. Tornado and hail formation increases dramatically in wetter regions, particularly across the South and lower Midwest, where atmospheric instability and moisture convergence create ideal storm conditions.
Coastal hazards and marine ecosystem disruption

The Pacific Coast faces a distinct set of hazards tied to El Niño's oceanic signature. High tide flooding accelerates along the West Coast as warmer ocean temperatures expand seawater and alter storm surge patterns, threatening ports, coastal infrastructure, and low-lying communities. This phenomenon has become increasingly predictable as climate observation networks from NOAA and UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography track sea-level rise linked to El Niño events.

The food insecurity crisis will not be uniform—different regions face vastly different levels of vulnerability based on their agricultural dependence and climate exposure.

As Patrick Kelly details in the episode , the consequences extend beyond hunger statistics to reshape supply chains for fresh produce globally. The warming Pacific waters already disrupt crop yields in some of the world's most critical agricultural regions.
Regional vulnerability and crop impacts

Central America's exposure is particularly acute, with the 83 percent increase in food insecurity representing a near-doubling of the crisis. The region's agricultural economy is heavily dependent on climate-sensitive crops , making it exceptionally vulnerable to the precipitation and temperature shifts El Niño brings.

East and South Africa, collectively facing 18 million people pushed into acute food insecurity, already struggle with fragile food systems. These regions will experience compounded stress from both crop failures and disrupted trade patterns. Southeast Asia and the broader Pacific region face equally severe threats to major staple crops, with global rice prices likely rising 10 to 20 percent due to yield losses alone.

f5286b474e.q: What are the expected impacts on global rice production and pricing due to El Niño conditions?
f5286b474e.a: El Niño is expected to reduce Indian and global rice yields, with global rice prices likely rising by 10 to 20 percent due to yield losses and tighter availability.

f: El Niño is expected to reduce Indian and global rice yields, with global rice prices likely rising by 10 to 20 percent due to yield losses and tighter availability. This price pressure will ripple through Southeast Asia and beyond, where rice is a critical staple crop and food security pillar.
Why rice yields face specific pressure from El Niño

Rice cultivation in major producing regions like India and Southeast Asia depends heavily on monsoon rainfall patterns and stable temperatures. El Niño disrupts both, typically bringing drier conditions to rice-growing areas during critical growth phases. As Patrick Kelly explains in the podcast episode , the forecasted strength of this El Niño event—with nearly 100 percent likelihood of persistence through February 2027—means yield stress will compound across multiple harvest cycles.

Lower production directly shrinks global supply, which historically triggers price spikes proportional to supply tightness . Rice markets, unlike other commodities, are tightly integrated into subsistence diets across developing nations, making price volatility politically and socially sensitive.
The food security cascade

Beyond pricing, the production decline feeds into a broader food insecurity crisis. The World Food Program estimates that El Niño-related shocks could push 49 million additional people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027, a figure that the episode explores across multiple regions and supply chain implications .

aea4b24a6a.q: What geographic regions face the highest drought and flooding risks from El Niño according to UN assessments?
aea4b24a6a.a: The UN warns that El Niño typically will elevate drought risk in Central America, Southeast Asia, the Sahel, and Southern Africa, while increasing flood hazards in East Africa and South America.
aea4b24a6a.e: Super El Niño Is Here: Weather, Crops & Global Food Risks
f: According to UN assessments cited in this episode , El Niño elevates drought risk in Central America, Southeast Asia, the Sahel, and Southern Africa , while simultaneously increasing flood hazards in East Africa and South America. These opposing weather impacts create a complex risk landscape that demands region-specific agricultural preparation.
Drought zones under El Niño pressure

The geographic footprint of El Niño-induced drought is remarkably consistent. Central America faces the most acute threat, with food insecurity rising by 83 percent in the region according to data discussed in the episode . This pattern reflects broader atmospheric circulation shifts driven by the weakening of the Walker Circulation—the ocean-atmosphere feedback system that normally steers weather patterns across the equatorial Pacific.

Southeast Asia and the Sahel—spanning West Africa's semi-arid belt—face similarly elevated drying conditions. Southern Africa completes the drought quadrant, a region whose agricultural output already carries outsized weight in global grain and commodity markets. When these four zones face simultaneous moisture stress, the cumulative crop stress ripples outward to affect global grain reserves and export corridors.
Simultaneous flooding in East Africa and South America

While drought grips four regions, El Niño simultaneously drives excess precipitation in East Africa and across parts of South America . This seemingly paradoxical pattern—drought and deluge on opposite sides of the Atlantic—reflects how El Niño disrupts the jet streams and moisture patterns that define normal seasonal weather.

Immediate pricing and yield pressures reshaping market dynamics

Supply chain complexity and cost escalation

Beyond pricing volatility, companies face rising operational and insurance costs as weather risk models worsen and carriers reprice their services. Shippers moving produce through disrupted corridors will encounter longer transit times, higher fuel surcharges, and pressure to secure air freight when ground logistics fail. Growers will see input costs rise as well—water scarcity drives irrigation expense, and pest pressure increases under warmer, wetter conditions.

Effects extending well beyond the peak
